caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Colombia's debt story is one of an oil exporter that never quite saved for the bust. The ratio was stable near 32-37% of GDP from 2006 through 2013 (36% in 2006, 34% in 2012), then jumped to 43.3% in 2014 and 50.4% in 2015 as the oil price collapse crushed revenues and the peso's depreciation revalued dollar debt. It hovered around 49-52% through 2019, then COVID pushed it to 65.3% in 2020, the series high; recovery brought it down to 55.4% in 2023 before it ticked back to 61% in 2024 and a projected 59.9% in 2025. Colombia lost its investment-grade ratings from S&P and Fitch in 2021 after deficit spending and the failed-then-revised tax reform, a downgrade that raised borrowing costs structurally. Dollar GDP grew from $161.8bn in 2006 to a projected $457.4bn in 2025, which has kept the ratio manageable, but the fiscal rule has been repeatedly strained.
inflation_management: The Banco de la Republica's inflation targeting (3% +/- 1 point) delivered mostly credible results: inflation ran 2-5.5% through 2015, with only the 2008 commodity spike (7%) breaking the band. The oil crash and 2015-16 El Nino drought pushed it to 7.5% in 2016, then it settled back to 3.2-4.3% in 2017-2021. The post-pandemic surge was severe: 10.2% in 2022 and 11.7% in 2023, the series high, driven by the peso, food prices, and regulated-price adjustments. Aggressive rate hikes brought it down to 6.6% in 2024 and a projected 5.1% in 2025 - still above target, making Colombia one of the slower disinflators in the region. The bank's willingness to hold rates high through 2024-25 preserved its credibility at the cost of growth.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis; Colombia weathered it better than most of the region.
Oil price collapse: crude was roughly half of exports; revenues plunged and the peso fell.
FARC peace accord signed and ratified in November, ending five decades of conflict.
Ivan Duque elected; tax reform attempts and social protests roiled 2019.
COVID-19; S&P and Fitch stripped Colombia of investment-grade status in 2021.
Gustavo Petro won in June, Colombia's first leftist president, on a reform platform.
Inflation peaked at 11.7% while Petro's tax reform and health reform advanced fitfully.
Fiscal pressures mounted ahead of the 2026 election; inflation projected at 5.1%.

outlook_next_decade: Colombia's outlook turns on two transitions: the 2026 presidential election and the long decline of oil as a fiscal pillar. The base case is continued gradual disinflation to target and debt stabilizing near 60% of GDP, with growth supported by nearshoring and infrastructure. The risks are fiscal - whether the next government restores a credible consolidation path after years of rule-bending - and security-related, as the peace process frays and coca production surges. Energy transition policy is the swing factor: faster diversification reduces oil dependence, but mishandled it raises the cost of the adjustment. Uncertainty is honestly high until the 2026 election clarifies the policy direction.
